Another thing to watch for is when inserting data from the client library, there is no comma between the two values, just a single space.\\\\n\\\\nAt this point, if you go into your Supabase dashboard and look at the data, you will notice that the value of the `location` column looks something like this.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n0101000020E6100000A4DFBE0E9C91614044FAEDEBC0494240\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWe can query the `restaurants` table directly, but it will return the `location` column in the format you see above.\\\\nWe will create [database functions](/docs/guides/database/functions) so that we can use the [st\\\\\\\\_y()](https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Y.html) and [st\\\\\\\\_x()](https://postgis.net/docs/ST_X.html) function to convert it back to lat and long floating values.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Order by distance\\\\n\\\\nSorting datasets from closest to farthest, sometimes called nearest-neighbor sort, is a very common use case in Geo-queries. PostGIS can handle it with the use of the [`<->`](https://postgis.net/docs/geometry_distance_knn.html) operator. `<->` operator returns the two-dimensional distance between two geometries and will utilize the spatial index when used within `order by` clause. You can create the following database function to sort the restaurants from closest to farthest by passing the current locations as parameters.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate or replace function nearby_restaurants(lat float, long float)\\\\nreturns table (id public.restaurants.id%TYPE, name public.restaurants.name%TYPE, lat float, long float, dist_meters float)\\\\nset search_path = ''\\\\nlanguage sql\\\\nas $$\\\\n  select id, name, extensions.st_y(location::extensions.geometry) as lat, extensions.st_x(location::extensions.geometry) as long, extensions.st_distance(location, extensions.st_point(long, lat)::extensions.geography) as dist_meters\\\\n  from public.restaurants\\\\n  order by location operator(extensions.<->) extensions.st_point(long, lat)::extensions.geography;\\\\n$$;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nNow you can call this function from your client using `rpc()` like this:\\\\n\\\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\\\\\"small\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"underlined\\\\\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\\\\\"js\\\\\\\" queryGroup=\\\\\\\"language\\\\\\\">\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"js\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"JavaScript\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```js\\\\n    const { data, error } = await supabase.rpc('nearby_restaurants', {\\\\n      lat: 40.807313,\\\\n      long: -73.946713,\\\\n    })\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"dart\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Dart\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```dart\\\\n    final data = await supabase.rpc('nearby_restaurants',params: {\\\\n      'lat': 40.807313,\\\\n      'long': -73.946713,\\\\n    });\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"swift\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Swift\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```swift\\\\n    struct Response: Codable {\\\\n      let id: Int\\\\n      let name: String\\\\n      let lat: Double\\\\n      let long: Double\\\\n      let distance: Double\\\\n\\\\n      enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey {\\\\n        case id, name, lat, long\\\\n        case distance = \\\\\\\"dist_meters\\\\\\\"\\\\n      }\\\\n    }\\\\n\\\\n    let response: Response = try await supabase.rpc(\\\\n      \\\\\\\"nearby_restaurants\\\\\\\",\\\\n      params: [\\\\n        \\\\\\\"lat\\\\\\\": 40.807313,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"long\\\\\\\": -73.946713\\\\n      ]\\\\n    )\\\\n    .execute()\\\\n    .value\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"kotlin\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Kotlin\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```kotlin\\\\n    val data = supabase.postgrest.rpc(\\\\n        function = \\\\\\\"nearby_restaurants\\\\\\\",\\\\n        parameters = buildJsonObject { //You can put here any serializable object including your own classes\\\\n            put(\\\\\\\"lat\\\\\\\", 40.807313)\\\\n            put(\\\\\\\"lon\\\\\\\", -73.946713)\\\\n        }\\\\n    )\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"result\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Result\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```json\\\\n    [\\\\n      {\\\\n        \\\\\\\"id\\\\\\\": 1,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Supa Burger\\\\\\\",\\\\n        \\\\\\\"lat\\\\\\\": 40.807416,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"long\\\\\\\": -73.946823,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"dist_meters\\\\\\\": 14.73033739\\\\n      },\\\\n      {\\\\n        \\\\\\\"id\\\\\\\": 2,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Supa Pizza\\\\\\\",\\\\n        \\\\\\\"lat\\\\\\\": 40.807475,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"long\\\\\\\": -73.94581,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"dist_meters\\\\\\\": 78.28980007\\\\n      },\\\\n      {\\\\n        \\\\\\\"id\\\\\\\": 3,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Supa Taco\\\\\\\",\\\\n        \\\\\\\"lat\\\\\\\": 40.80629,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"long\\\\\\\": -73.945826,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"dist_meters\\\\\\\": 136.04329002\\\\n      }\\\\n    ]\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n</Tabs>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Finding all data points within a bounding box\\\\n\\\\n![Searching within a bounding box of a map](/docs/img/guides/database/extensions/postgis/map.png)\\\\n\\\\nWhen you are working on a map-based application where the user scrolls through your map, you might want to load the data that lies within the bounding box of the map every time your users scroll. PostGIS can return the rows that are within the bounding box just by supplying the bottom left and the top right coordinates. Let\\u2019s look at what the function would look like:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate or replace function restaurants_in_view(min_lat float, min_long float, max_lat float, max_long float)\\\\nreturns table (id public.restaurants.id%TYPE, name public.restaurants.name%TYPE, lat float, long float)\\\\nset search_path to ''\\\\nlanguage sql\\\\nas $$\\\\n\\\\tselect id, name, extensions.st_y(location::extensions.geometry) as lat, extensions.st_x(location::extensions.geometry) as long\\\\n\\\\tfrom public.restaurants\\\\n\\\\twhere location operator(extensions.&&) extensions.ST_SetSRID(extensions.ST_MakeBox2D(extensions.ST_Point(min_long, min_lat), extensions.ST_Point(max_long, max_lat)), 4326)\\\\n$$;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe [`&&`](https://postgis.net/docs/geometry_overlaps.html) operator used in the `where` statement here returns a boolean of whether the bounding box of the two geometries intersect or not. We are basically creating a bounding box from the two points and finding those points that fall under the bounding box. We are also utilizing a few different PostGIS functions:\\\\n\\\\n*   [ST\\\\\\\\_MakeBox2D](https://postgis.net/docs/ST_MakeBox2D.html): Creates a 2-dimensional box from two points.\\\\n*   [ST\\\\\\\\_SetSRID](https://postgis.net/docs/ST_SetSRID.html): Sets the [SRID](https://postgis.net/docs/manual-dev/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#spatial_ref_sys), which is an identifier of what coordinate system to use for the geometry. 4326 is the standard longitude and latitude coordinate system.\\\\n\\\\nYou can call this function from your client using `rpc()` like this:\\\\n\\\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\\\\\"small\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"underlined\\\\\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\\\\\"js\\\\\\\" queryGroup=\\\\\\\"language\\\\\\\">\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"js\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"JavaScript\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```js\\\\n    const { data, error } = await supabase.rpc('restaurants_in_view', {\\\\n      min_lat: 40.807,\\\\n      min_long: -73.946,\\\\n      max_lat: 40.808,\\\\n      max_long: -73.945,\\\\n    })\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"dart\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Dart\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```dart\\\\n    final data = await supabase.rpc('restaurants_in_view', params: {\\\\n      'min_lat': 40.807,\\\\n      'min_long': -73.946,\\\\n      'max_lat': 40.808,\\\\n      'max_long': -73.945,\\\\n    });\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"swift\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Swift\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```swift\\\\n    struct Response: Codable {\\\\n      let id: Int\\\\n      let name: String\\\\n      let lat: Double\\\\n      let long: Double\\\\n    }\\\\n\\\\n    let response: Response = try await supabase.rpc(\\\\n      \\\\\\\"restaurants_in_view\\\\\\\",\\\\n      params: [\\\\n        \\\\\\\"min_lat\\\\\\\": 40.807,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"min_long\\\\\\\": -73.946,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"max_long\\\\\\\": -73.945,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"max_lat\\\\\\\": 40.808,\\\\n      ]\\\\n    )\\\\n    .execute()\\\\n    .value\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"kotlin\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Kotlin\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```kotlin\\\\n    val data = supabase.postgrest.rpc(\\\\n        function = \\\\\\\"restaurants_in_view\\\\\\\",\\\\n        parameters = buildJsonObject { //You can put here any serializable object including your own classes\\\\n            put(\\\\\\\"min_lat\\\\\\\", 40.807)\\\\n            put(\\\\\\\"min_lon\\\\\\\", -73.946)\\\\n            put(\\\\\\\"max_lat\\\\\\\", 40.808)\\\\n            put(\\\\\\\"max_lon\\\\\\\", -73.945)\\\\n        }\\\\n    )\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"result\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Result\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```json\\\\n    [\\\\n      {\\\\n        \\\\\\\"id\\\\\\\": 2,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Supa Pizza\\\\\\\",\\\\n        \\\\\\\"lat\\\\\\\": 40.807475,\\\\n        \\\\\\\"long\\\\\\\": -73.94581\\\\n      }\\\\n    ]\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n</Tabs>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Troubleshooting\\\\n\\\\nAs of PostGIS 2.3 or newer, the PostGIS extension is no longer relocatable from one schema to another. If you need to move it from one schema to another for any reason (e.g. from the public schema to the extensions schema for security reasons), you would normally run a ALTER EXTENSION to relocate the schema. However, you will now to do the following steps:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Backup your Database to prevent data loss - You can do this through the [CLI](/docs/reference/cli/supabase-db-dump) or Postgres backup tools such as [pg\\\\\\\\_dumpall](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/backup-dump.html#BACKUP-DUMP-ALL)\\\\n\\\\n2.  Drop all dependencies you created and the PostGIS extension - `DROP EXTENSION postgis CASCADE;`\\\\n\\\\n3.  Enable PostGIS extension in the new schema - `CREATE EXTENSION postgis SCHEMA extensions;`\\\\n\\\\n4.  Restore dropped data via the Backup if necessary from step 1 with your tool of choice.\\\\n\\\\nAlternatively, you can contact the [Supabase Support Team](/dashboard/support/new) and ask them to run the following SQL on your instance:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nBEGIN;\\\\n\\\\tUPDATE pg_extension\\\\n\\\\t  SET extrelocatable = true\\\\n\\\\tWHERE extname = 'postgis';\\\\n\\\\n\\\\tALTER EXTENSION postgis\\\\n\\\\t  SET SCHEMA extensions;\\\\n\\\\n\\\\tALTER EXTENSION postgis\\\\n\\\\t  UPDATE TO \\\\\\\"<POSTGIS_VERSION>next\\\\\\\";\\\\n\\\\n\\\\tALTER EXTENSION postgis UPDATE;\\\\n\\\\n\\\\tUPDATE pg_extension\\\\n\\\\t  SET extrelocatable = false\\\\n\\\\tWHERE extname = 'postgis';\\\\nCOMMIT;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Resources\\\\n\\\\n*   [Official PostGIS documentation](https://postgis.net/documentation/)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Hardening the Data API\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/hardening-data-api\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Hardening the Data API\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nYour database's auto-generated Data API exposes the `public` schema by default. You can change this to any schema in your database, or even disable the Data API completely.\\\\n\\\\nAny tables that are accessible through the Data API *must* have [Row Level Security](/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) enabled. Row Level Security (RLS) is enabled by default when you create tables from the Supabase Dashboard. If you create a table using the SQL editor or your own SQL client or migration runner, you*must* enable RLS yourself.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Shared responsibility\\\\n\\\\nYour application's security is your responsibility as a developer. This includes RLS, falling under the [Shared Responsibility](/docs/guides/deployment/shared-responsibility-model) model. To help you:\\\\n\\\\n*   Supabase sends daily emails warning of any tables that are exposed to the Data API which do not have RLS enabled.\\\\n*   Supabase provides a Security Advisor and other tools in the Supabase Dashboard to fix any issues.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Private schemas\\\\n\\\\nWe highly recommend creating a `private` schema for storing tables that you do not want to expose via the Data API. These tables can be accessed via Supabase Edge Functions or any other serverside tool. In this model, you should implement your security model in your serverside code. Although it's not required, we *still* recommend enabling RLS for private tables and then connecting to your database using a Postgres role with `bypassrls` privileges.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Managing the public schema\\\\n\\\\nIf your `public` schema is used by other tools as a default space, you might want to lock down this schema. This helps prevent accidental exposure of data that's automatically added to `public`.\\\\n\\\\nThere are two levels of security hardening for the Data API:\\\\n\\\\n*   Disabling the Data API entirely. This is recommended if you *never* need to access your database via Supabase client libraries or the REST and GraphQL endpoints.\\\\n*   Removing the `public` schema from the Data API and replacing it with a custom schema (such as `api`).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Disabling the Data API\\\\n\\\\nYou can disable the Data API entirely if you never intend to use the Supabase client libraries or the REST and GraphQL data endpoints. For example, if you only access your database via a direct connection on the server, disabling the Data API gives you the greatest layer of protection.\\\\n\\\\n1.  Go to [API Settings](/dashboard/project/_/settings/api) in the Supabase Dashboard.\\\\n2.  Under **Data API Settings**, toggle **Enable Data API** off.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Exposing a custom schema instead of `public`\\\\n\\\\nIf you want to use the Data API but with increased security, you can expose a custom schema instead of `public`. By not using `public`, which is often used as a default space and has laxer default permissions, you get more conscious control over your exposed data.\\\\n\\\\nAny data, views, or functions that should be exposed need to be deliberately put within your custom schema (which we will call `api`), rather than ending up there by default.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 1: Remove `public` from exposed schemas\\\\n\\\\n1.  Go to [**API Settings**](/dashboard/project/_/settings/api) in the Supabase Dashboard.\\\\n2.  Under **Data API Settings**, remove `public` from **Exposed schemas**. Also remove `public` from **Extra search path**.\\\\n3.  Click **Save**.\\\\n4.  Go to [**Database Extensions**](/dashboard/project/_/database/extensions) and disable the `pg_graphql` extension.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 2: Create an `api` schema and expose it\\\\n\\\\n1.  Connect to your database. You can use `psql`, the [Supabase SQL Editor](/dashboard/project/_/sql), or the Postgres client of your choice.\\\\n\\\\n2.  Create a new schema named `api`:\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    create schema if not exists api;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\\n3.  Grant the `anon` and `authenticated` roles usage on this schema.\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    grant usage on schema api to anon, authenticated;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\\n4.  Go to [API Settings](/dashboard/project/_/settings/api) in the Supabase Dashboard.\\\\n\\\\n5.  Under **Data API Settings**, add `api` to **Exposed schemas**. Make sure it is the first schema in the list, so that it will be searched first by default.\\\\n\\\\n6.  Under these new settings, `anon` and `authenticated` can execute functions defined in the `api` schema, but they have no automatic permissions on any tables. On a table-by-table basis, you can grant them permissions. For example:\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    grant select on table api.<your_table> to anon;\\\\n    grant select, insert, update, delete on table api.<your_table> to authenticated;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"REST API\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# REST API\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nSupabase auto-generates an API directly from your database schema allowing you to connect to your database through a restful interface, directly from the browser.\\\\n\\\\nThe API is auto-generated from your database and is designed to get you building as fast as possible, without writing a single line of code.\\\\n\\\\nYou can use them directly from the browser (two-tier architecture), or as a complement to your own API server (three-tier architecture).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Features \\\\\\\\[#rest-api-overview]\\\\n\\\\nSupabase provides a RESTful API using [PostgREST](https://postgrest.org/). This is a very thin API layer on top of Postgres.\\\\nIt exposes everything you need from a CRUD API at the URL `https://<project_ref>.supabase.co/rest/v1/`.\\\\n\\\\nThe REST interface is automatically reflected from your database's schema and is:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Instant and auto-generated.** <br />As you update your database the changes are immediately accessible through your API.\\\\n*   **Self documenting.** <br />Supabase generates documentation in the Dashboard which updates as you make database changes.\\\\n*   **Secure.** <br />The API is configured to work with PostgreSQL's Row Level Security, provisioned behind an API gateway with key-auth enabled.\\\\n*   **Fast.** <br />Our benchmarks for basic reads are more than 300% faster than Firebase. The API is a very thin layer on top of Postgres, which does most of the heavy lifting.\\\\n*   **Scalable.** <br />The API can serve thousands of simultaneous requests, and works well for Serverless workloads.\\\\n\\\\nThe reflected API is designed to retain as much of Postgres' capability as possible including:\\\\n\\\\n*   Basic CRUD operations (Create/Read/Update/Delete)\\\\n*   Arbitrarily deep relationships among tables/views, functions that return table types can also nest related tables/views.\\\\n*   Works with Postgres Views, Materialized Views and Foreign Tables\\\\n*   Works with Postgres Functions\\\\n*   User defined computed columns and computed relationships\\\\n*   The Postgres security model - including Row Level Security, Roles, and Grants.\\\\n\\\\nThe REST API resolves all requests to a single SQL statement leading to fast response times and high throughput.\\\\n\\\\nReference:\\\\n\\\\n*   [Docs](https://postgrest.org/)\\\\n*   [Source Code](https://github.com/PostgREST/postgrest)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## API URL and keys\\\\n\\\\nYou can find the API URL and Keys in the [Dashboard](/dashboard/project/_/settings/api-keys).\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"pg_jsonschema: JSON Schema Validation\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/extensions/pg_jsonschema\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# pg_jsonschema: JSON Schema Validation\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n[JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org) is a language for annotating and validating JSON documents. [`pg_jsonschema`](https://github.com/supabase/pg_jsonschema) is a Postgres extension that adds the ability to validate PostgreSQL's built-in `json` and `jsonb` data types against JSON Schema documents.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Enable the extension\\\\n\\\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\\\\\"small\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"underlined\\\\\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\\\\\"dashboard\\\\\\\" queryGroup=\\\\\\\"database-method\\\\\\\">\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"dashboard\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Dashboard\\\\\\\">\\\\n    1.  Go to the [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/tables) page in the Dashboard.\\\\n    2.  Click on **Extensions** in the sidebar.\\\\n    3.  Search for `pg_jsonschema` and enable the extension.\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"sql\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"SQL\\\\\\\">\\\\n    {/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    -- Enable the \\\\\\\"pg_jsonschema\\\\\\\" extension\\\\n    create extension pg_jsonschema with schema extensions;\\\\n\\\\n    -- Disable the \\\\\\\"pg_jsonschema\\\\\\\" extension\\\\n    drop extension if exists pg_jsonschema;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\\n    Even though the SQL code is `create extension`, this is the equivalent of enabling the extension.\\\\n    To disable an extension you can call `drop extension`.\\\\n\\\\n    It's good practice to create the extension within a separate schema (like `extensions`) to keep the `public` schema clean.\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n</Tabs>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Functions\\\\n\\\\n*   [`json_matches_schema(schema json, instance json)`](https://github.com/supabase/pg_jsonschema#api): Checks if a `json` *instance* conforms to a JSON Schema *schema*.\\\\n*   [`jsonb_matches_schema(schema json, instance jsonb)`](https://github.com/supabase/pg_jsonschema#api): Checks if a `jsonb` *instance* conforms to a JSON Schema *schema*.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Usage\\\\n\\\\nSince `pg_jsonschema` exposes its utilities as functions, we can execute them with a select statement:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nselect\\\\n  extensions.json_matches_schema(\\\\n    schema := '{\\\\\\\"type\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"object\\\\\\\"}',\\\\n    instance := '{}'\\\\n  );\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`pg_jsonschema` is generally used in tandem with a [check constraint](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html) as a way to constrain the contents of a json/b column to match a JSON Schema.\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate table customer(\\\\n    id serial primary key,\\\\n    ...\\\\n    metadata json,\\\\n\\\\n    check (\\\\n        json_matches_schema(\\\\n            '{\\\\n                \\\\\\\"type\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"object\\\\\\\",\\\\n                \\\\\\\"properties\\\\\\\": {\\\\n                    \\\\\\\"tags\\\\\\\": {\\\\n                        \\\\\\\"type\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"array\\\\\\\",\\\\n                        \\\\\\\"items\\\\\\\": {\\\\n                            \\\\\\\"type\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"string\\\\\\\",\\\\n                            \\\\\\\"maxLength\\\\\\\": 16\\\\n                        }\\\\n                    }\\\\n                }\\\\n            }',\\\\n            metadata\\\\n        )\\\\n    )\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\n-- Example: Valid Payload\\\\ninsert into customer(metadata)\\\\nvalues ('{\\\\\\\"tags\\\\\\\": [\\\\\\\"vip\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"darkmode-ui\\\\\\\"]}');\\\\n-- Result:\\\\n--   INSERT 0 1\\\\n\\\\n-- Example: Invalid Payload\\\\ninsert into customer(metadata)\\\\nvalues ('{\\\\\\\"tags\\\\\\\": [1, 3]}');\\\\n-- Result:\\\\n--   ERROR:  new row for relation \\\\\\\"customer\\\\\\\" violates check constraint \\\\\\\"customer_metadata_check\\\\\\\"\\\\n--   DETAIL:  Failing row contains (2, {\\\\\\\"tags\\\\\\\": [1, 3]}).\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Resources\\\\n\\\\n*   Official [`pg_jsonschema` documentation](https://github.com/supabase/pg_jsonschema)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Realtime Authorization\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/authorization\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Realtime Authorization\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nYou can control client access to Realtime [Broadcast](/docs/guides/realtime/broadcast) and [Presence](/docs/guides/realtime/presence) by adding Row Level Security policies to the `realtime.messages` table. Each RLS policy can map to a specific action a client can take:\\\\n\\\\n*   Control which clients can broadcast to a Channel\\\\n*   Control which clients can receive broadcasts from a Channel\\\\n*   Control which clients can publish their presence to a Channel\\\\n*   Control which clients can receive messages about the presence of other clients\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"caution\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Realtime Authorization is in Public Beta. To use Authorization for your Realtime Channels, use `supabase-js` version `v2.44.0` or later.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  To enforce private channels you need to disable the 'Allow public access' setting in [Realtime Settings](/dashboard/project/_/realtime/settings)\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## How it works\\\\n\\\\nRealtime uses the `messages` table in your database's `realtime` schema to generate access policies for your clients when they connect to a Channel topic.\\\\n\\\\nBy creating RLS policies on the `realtime.messages` table you can control the access users have to a Channel topic, and features within a Channel topic.\\\\n\\\\nThe validation is done when the user connects. When their WebSocket connection is established and a Channel topic is joined, their permissions are calculated based on:\\\\n\\\\n*   The RLS policies on the `realtime.messages` table\\\\n*   The user information sent as part of their [Auth JWT](/docs/guides/auth/jwts)\\\\n*   The request headers\\\\n*   The Channel topic the user is trying to connect to\\\\n\\\\nWhen Realtime generates a policy for a client it performs a query on the `realtime.messages` table and then rolls it back. Realtime does not store any messages in your `realtime.messages` table.\\\\n\\\\nUsing Realtime Authorization involves two steps:\\\\n\\\\n*   In your database, create RLS policies on the `realtime.messages`\\\\n*   In your client, instantiate the Realtime Channel with the `config` option `private: true`\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"caution\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Increased RLS complexity can impact database performance and connection time, leading to higher connection latency and decreased join rates.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Accessing request information\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `realtime.topic`\\\\n\\\\nYou can use the `realtime.topic` helper function when writing RLS policies. It returns the Channel topic the user is attempting to connect to.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated can read all messages on topic\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor select\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nusing (\\\\n  (select realtime.topic()) = 'room-1'\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### JWT claims\\\\n\\\\nThe user claims can be accessed using the `current_setting` function. The claims are available as a JSON object in the `request.jwt.claims` setting.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated with supabase.io email can read all\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor select\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nusing (\\\\n  -- Only users with the email claim ending with @supabase.io\\\\n  (((current_setting('request.jwt.claims'))::json ->> 'email') ~~ '%@supabase.io')\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Examples\\\\n\\\\nThe following examples use this schema:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate table public.rooms (\\\\n    id bigint generated by default as identity primary key,\\\\n    topic text not null unique\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\nalter table public.rooms enable row level security;\\\\n\\\\ncreate table public.profiles (\\\\n  id uuid not null references auth.users on delete cascade,\\\\n  email text NOT NULL,\\\\n\\\\n  primary key (id)\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\nalter table public.profiles enable row level security;\\\\n\\\\ncreate table public.rooms_users (\\\\n  user_id uuid references auth.users (id),\\\\n  room_topic text references public.rooms (topic),\\\\n  created_at timestamptz default current_timestamp\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\nalter table public.rooms_users enable row level security;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Broadcast\\\\n\\\\nThe `extension` field on the `realtime.messages` table records the message type. For Broadcast messages, the value of `realtime.messages.extension` is `broadcast`. You can check for this in your RLS policies.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Allow a user to join (and read) a Broadcast topic\\\\n\\\\nTo join a Broadcast Channel, a user must have at least one read or write permission on the Channel topic.\\\\n\\\\nHere, we allow reads (`select`s) for users who are linked to the requested topic within the relationship table `public.room_users`:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated can receive broadcast\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor select\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nusing (\\\\nexists (\\\\n    select\\\\n      user_id\\\\n    from\\\\n      rooms_users\\\\n    where\\\\n      user_id = (select auth.uid())\\\\n      and topic = (select realtime.topic())\\\\n      and realtime.messages.extension in ('broadcast')\\\\n  )\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThen, to join a topic with RLS enabled, instantiate the Channel with the `private` option set to `true`.\\\\n\\\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\\\\\"small\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"underlined\\\\\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\\\\\"js\\\\\\\" queryGroup=\\\\\\\"language\\\\\\\">\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"js\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"JavaScript\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```javascript\\\\n    import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'\\\\n    const supabase = createClient('your_project_url', 'your_supabase_api_key')\\\\n\\\\n    // ---cut---\\\\n    const channel = supabase.channel('room-1', {\\\\n      config: { private: true },\\\\n    })\\\\n\\\\n    channel\\\\n      .on('broadcast', { event: 'test' }, (payload) => console.log(payload))\\\\n      .subscribe((status, err) => {\\\\n        if (status === 'SUBSCRIBED') {\\\\n          console.log('Connected!')\\\\n        } else {\\\\n          console.error(err)\\\\n        }\\\\n      })\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"dart\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Dart\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```dart\\\\n    final channel = supabase.channel(\\\\n      'room-1',\\\\n      opts: const RealtimeChannelConfig(private: true),\\\\n    );\\\\n\\\\n    channel\\\\n        .onBroadcast(event: 'test', callback: (payload) => print(payload))\\\\n        .subscribe((status, err) {\\\\n      if (status == RealtimeSubscribeStatus.subscribed) {\\\\n        print('Connected!');\\\\n      } else {\\\\n        print(err);\\\\n      }\\\\n    });\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"swift\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Swift\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```swift\\\\n    let channel = supabase.channel(\\\\\\\"room-1\\\\\\\") {\\\\n      $0.isPrivate = true\\\\n    }\\\\n\\\\n    Task {\\\\n      for await payload in channel.broadcastStream(event: \\\\\\\"test\\\\\\\") {\\\\n        print(payload)\\\\n      }\\\\n    }\\\\n\\\\n    await channel.subscribe()\\\\n    print(\\\\\\\"Connected!\\\\\\\")\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"kotlin\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Kotlin\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```kotlin\\\\n    val channel = supabase.channel(\\\\\\\"room-1\\\\\\\") {\\\\n        isPrivate = true\\\\n    }\\\\n    channel.broadcastFlow<MyPayload>(event = \\\\\\\"test\\\\\\\").onEach {\\\\n        println(it)\\\\n    }.launchIn(scope) // launch in your coroutine scope\\\\n    channel.subscribe(blockUntilSubscribed = true)\\\\n    println(\\\\\\\"Connected!\\\\\\\")\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"python\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Python\\\\\\\">\\\\n    ```py\\\\n    channel = realtime.channel(\\\\n      \\\\\\\"room-1\\\\\\\", {\\\\\\\"config\\\\\\\": {\\\\\\\"private\\\\\\\": True}}\\\\n    )\\\\n\\\\n    await channel.on_broadcast(\\\\n      \\\\\\\"test\\\\\\\", callback=lambda payload: print(payload)\\\\n    ).subscribe(\\\\n      lambda state, err: (\\\\n        print(\\\\\\\"Connected\\\\\\\")\\\\n        if state == RealtimeSubscribeStates.SUBSCRIBED\\\\n        else print(err)\\\\n      )\\\\n    )\\\\n    ```\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n</Tabs>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Allow a user to send a Broadcast message\\\\n\\\\nTo authorize sending Broadcast messages, create a policy for `insert` where the value of `realtime.messages.extension` is `broadcast`.\\\\n\\\\nHere, we allow writes (sends) for users who are linked to the requested topic within the relationship table `public.room_users`:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated can send broadcast on topic\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor insert\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nwith check (\\\\n  exists (\\\\n    select\\\\n      user_id\\\\n    from\\\\n      rooms_users\\\\n    where\\\\n      user_id = (select auth.uid())\\\\n      and topic = (select realtime.topic())\\\\n      and realtime.messages.extension in ('broadcast')\\\\n  )\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Presence\\\\n\\\\nThe `extension` field on the `realtime.messages` table records the message type. For Presence messages, the value of `realtime.messages.extension` is `presence`. You can check for this in your RLS policies.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Allow users to listen to Presence messages on a Channel\\\\n\\\\nCreate a policy for `select` on `realtime.messages` where `realtime.messages.extension` is `presence`.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated can listen to presence in topic\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor select\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nusing (\\\\n  exists (\\\\n    select\\\\n      user_id\\\\n    from\\\\n      rooms_users\\\\n    where\\\\n      user_id = (select auth.uid())\\\\n      and topic = (select realtime.topic())\\\\n      and realtime.messages.extension in ('presence')\\\\n  )\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Allow users to send Presence messages on a channel\\\\n\\\\nTo update the Presence status for a user create a policy for `insert` on `realtime.messages` where the value of `realtime.messages.extension` is `presence`.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated can track presence on topic\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor insert\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nwith check (\\\\n  exists (\\\\n    select\\\\n      user_id\\\\n    from\\\\n      rooms_users\\\\n    where\\\\n      user_id = (select auth.uid())\\\\n      and name = (select realtime.topic())\\\\n      and realtime.messages.extension in ('presence')\\\\n  )\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Presence and Broadcast\\\\n\\\\nAuthorize both Presence and Broadcast by including both extensions in the `where` filter.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Broadcast and Presence read\\\\n\\\\nAuthorize Presence and Broadcast read in one RLS policy.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated can listen to broadcast and presence on topic\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor select\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nusing (\\\\n  exists (\\\\n    select\\\\n      user_id\\\\n    from\\\\n      rooms_users\\\\n    where\\\\n      user_id = (select auth.uid())\\\\n      and topic = (select realtime.topic())\\\\n      and realtime.messages.extension in ('broadcast', 'presence')\\\\n  )\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Broadcast and Presence write\\\\n\\\\nAuthorize Presence and Broadcast write in one RLS policy.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate policy \\\\\\\"authenticated can send broadcast and presence on topic\\\\\\\"\\\\non \\\\\\\"realtime\\\\\\\".\\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\"\\\\nfor insert\\\\nto authenticated\\\\nwith check (\\\\n  exists (\\\\n    select\\\\n      user_id\\\\n    from\\\\n      rooms_users\\\\n    where\\\\n      user_id = (select auth.uid())\\\\n      and name = (select realtime.topic())\\\\n      and realtime.messages.extension in ('broadcast', 'presence')\\\\n  )\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Interaction with Postgres Changes\\\\n\\\\nRealtime Postgres Changes are separate from Channel authorization. The `private` Channel option does not apply to Postgres Changes.\\\\n\\\\nWhen using Postgres Changes with RLS, database records are sent only to clients who are allowed to read them based on your RLS policies.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Updating RLS policies\\\\n\\\\nClient access policies are cached for the duration of the connection. Your database is not queried for every Channel message.\\\\n\\\\nRealtime updates the access policy cache for a client based on your RLS policies when:\\\\n\\\\n*   A client connects to Realtime and subscribes to a Channel\\\\n*   A new JWT is sent to Realtime from a client via the [`access_token` message](/docs/guides/realtime/protocol#access-token)\\\\n\\\\nIf a new JWT is never received on the Channel, the client will be disconnected when the JWT expires.\\\\n\\\\nMake sure to keep the JWT expiration window short.\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Replication Setup\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-setup\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Replication Setup\\\\n\\\\nConfigure publications and destinations for replication.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"caution\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Private Alpha\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Replication is currently in private alpha. Access is limited and features may change.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\nReplication uses **Postgres logical replication** to stream changes from your database. Powered by [Supabase ETL](https://github.com/supabase/etl), an open source tool built for Postgres logical replication, it provides a managed interface through the Dashboard to configure and monitor replication pipelines.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Setup overview\\\\n\\\\nReplication requires two main components: a **Postgres publication** (defines what to replicate) and a **destination** (where data is sent). Follow these steps to set up your replication pipeline.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"tip\\\\\\\">\\\\n  If you already have a Postgres publication set up, you can skip to [Step 2: Enable replication](#step-2-enable-replication).\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 1: Create a Postgres publication\\\\n\\\\nA Postgres publication defines which tables and change types will be replicated from your database. You create publications using SQL.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Creating a publication\\\\n\\\\nThe following SQL examples assume you have `users` and `orders` tables in your database.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Publication for specific tables\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create publication for both tables\\\\ncreate publication pub_users_orders\\\\nfor table users, orders;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis publication will track all changes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE) for both the `users` and `orders` tables.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Publication for all tables in a schema\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create a publication for all tables in the public schema\\\\ncreate publication pub_all_public for tables in schema public;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will track changes for all existing and future tables in the `public` schema.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Publication for all tables\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create a publication for all tables\\\\ncreate publication pub_all_tables for all tables;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will track changes for all tables in your database.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Advanced publication options\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Selecting specific columns\\\\n\\\\nYou can replicate only a subset of columns from a table:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Replicate only specific columns from the users table\\\\ncreate publication pub_users_subset\\\\nfor table users (id, email, created_at);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will only replicate the `id`, `email`, and `created_at` columns from the `users` table.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Filtering rows with a predicate\\\\n\\\\nYou can filter which rows to replicate using a WHERE clause:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Only replicate active users\\\\ncreate publication pub_active_users\\\\nfor table users where (status = 'active');\\\\n\\\\n-- Only replicate recent orders\\\\ncreate publication pub_recent_orders\\\\nfor table orders where (created_at > '2024-01-01');\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Viewing publications in the Dashboard\\\\n\\\\nAfter creating a publication via SQL, you can view it in the Supabase Dashboard:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Navigate to **Database** \\u2192 [Publications](/dashboard/project/_/database/publications) in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n2.  You'll see all your publications listed with their tables\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 2: Enable replication\\\\n\\\\nBefore adding destinations, you need to enable replication for your project:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Navigate to the [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/replication) section in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n2.  Select the **replication** tab\\\\n3.  Click **Enable replication** to activate replication for your project\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"Enable Replication\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-enable-replication.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 3: Add a destination\\\\n\\\\nOnce replication is enabled and you have a Postgres publication, you can add a destination. The destination is where your replicated data will be stored, while the pipeline is the active Postgres replication process that continuously streams changes from your database to that destination.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Choose and configure your destination\\\\n\\\\nFollow these steps to configure your destination. The specific configuration depends on which destination type you choose. Both Analytics Buckets and BigQuery destinations are supported, though availability varies based on the planned roll-out strategy.\\\\n\\\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\\\\\"small\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"underlined\\\\\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\\\\\"analytics-buckets\\\\\\\" queryGroup=\\\\\\\"destination\\\\\\\">\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"analytics-buckets\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Analytics Buckets\\\\\\\">\\\\n    [Analytics Buckets](/docs/guides/storage/analytics/introduction) are specialized storage buckets in Supabase Storage designed for analytical workloads. They provide S3-compatible storage and use the [Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/) open table format, making your data accessible via standard tools like DuckDB, Spark, and other analytics platforms.\\\\n\\\\n    When you replicate to Analytics Buckets, your database changes are automatically written in Iceberg format, creating tables in object storage that you can query for analytics.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 1: Create an analytics bucket\\\\n\\\\n    First, create an analytics bucket to store your replicated data:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Navigate to [Storage](/dashboard/project/_/storage/buckets) \\u2192 **Analytics** in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n\\\\n    2.  Click **New bucket**\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"Create new analytics bucket\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-iceberg-new-bucket.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n    3.  Fill in the bucket details:\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"Analytics bucket details\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-iceberg-details.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Name**: A unique name for your bucket (e.g., `analytics_warehouse`)\\\\n        *   **Region**: Select the region where your data will be stored\\\\n\\\\n    4.  Click **Create bucket**\\\\n\\\\n    5.  **Copy the credentials** displayed after bucket creation. You'll need these in the next steps:\\\\n        *   **Catalog Token**: Authentication token for accessing the Iceberg catalog\\\\n        *   **S3 Access Key ID**: Access key for S3-compatible storage\\\\n        *   **S3 Secret Access Key**: Secret key for S3-compatible storage\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 2: Configure analytics buckets as a destination\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Navigate to [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/replication) \\u2192 **replication** in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n\\\\n    2.  Click **Add destination**\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"Add Destination\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-add-destination.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n    3.  Configure the general settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Destination name**: A name to identify this destination (e.g., \\\\\\\"Analytics Warehouse\\\\\\\")\\\\n        *   **Publication**: The publication to replicate data from (created in [Step 1](#step-1-create-a-postgres-publication))\\\\n        *   **Destination type**: Select **Analytics Buckets**\\\\n\\\\n    4.  Configure Analytics Buckets settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Bucket**: The name of your analytics bucket from Step 1\\\\n        *   **Namespace**: The schema name where your tables will be replicated (e.g., `public`)\\\\n        *   **Catalog Token**: Authentication token from Step 1\\\\n        *   **S3 Access Key ID**: Access key from Step 1\\\\n        *   **S3 Secret Access Key**: Secret key from Step 1\\\\n\\\\n    5.  Configure **Advanced Settings** (optional):\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Batch wait time (milliseconds)**: How long to wait for more changes before sending a batch. Default is recommended for optimal performance.\\\\n\\\\n    6.  Click **Create and start** to begin replication\\\\n\\\\n    Your replication pipeline will now start copying data from your database to the analytics bucket in Iceberg format.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How it works\\\\n\\\\n    Once configured, replication to Analytics Buckets:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Captures changes from your Postgres database (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE operations)\\\\n    2.  Batches changes for optimal performance\\\\n    3.  Creates Iceberg tables automatically to match your Postgres schema\\\\n    4.  Streams data to Analytics Buckets\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How tables are structured\\\\n\\\\n    Replicated tables use a changelog structure:\\\\n\\\\n    *   Tables are created with a `_changelog` suffix in the name (e.g., `users_changelog`)\\\\n    *   Each table contains a `cdc_operation` column indicating the operation type: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, or `TRUNCATE`\\\\n    *   This append-only format preserves the complete history of all changes\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Limitations\\\\n\\\\n    *   **Append-only log**: Currently provides an append-only log format rather than a full table representation\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Additional resources\\\\n\\\\n    *   [Analytics Buckets documentation](/docs/guides/storage/analytics/introduction) - Learn more about Analytics Buckets and S3-compatible storage\\\\n    *   [Realtime Data Sync to Analytics Buckets](/docs/guides/storage/analytics/replication) - Step-by-step guide for replicating to Analytics Buckets\\\\n    *   [Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/) - Official Iceberg documentation\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"bigquery\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"BigQuery\\\\\\\">\\\\n    [BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery) is Google's fully managed data warehouse. You can replicate your database tables to BigQuery for analytics and reporting.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 1: Prepare GCP resources\\\\n\\\\n    Before configuring BigQuery as a destination, set up the following in Google Cloud Platform:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  **Google Cloud Platform (GCP) account**: [Sign up for GCP](https://cloud.google.com/gcp) if you don't have one\\\\n\\\\n    2.  **BigQuery dataset**: Create a [BigQuery dataset](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/datasets-intro) in your GCP project\\\\n\\\\n        *   Open the BigQuery console in GCP\\\\n        *   Select your project\\\\n        *   Click \\\\\\\"Create Dataset\\\\\\\"\\\\n        *   Provide a dataset ID (e.g., `supabase_replication`)\\\\n\\\\n    3.  **GCP service account key**: Create a [service account](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/keys-create-delete) with appropriate permissions:\\\\n\\\\n        *   Go to IAM & Admin \\u2192 Service Accounts\\\\n        *   Click \\\\\\\"Create Service Account\\\\\\\"\\\\n        *   Grant the **BigQuery Data Editor** role\\\\n        *   Create and download the JSON key file\\\\n\\\\n        Required permissions:\\\\n\\\\n        *   `bigquery.datasets.get`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.create`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.get`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.getData`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.update`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.updateData`\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 2: Configure BigQuery as a destination\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Navigate to [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/replication) \\u2192 **replication** in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n\\\\n    2.  Click **Add destination**\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"BigQuery Configuration Settings\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-bigquery-details.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n    3.  Configure the general settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Destination name**: A name to identify this destination (e.g., \\\\\\\"BigQuery Warehouse\\\\\\\")\\\\n        *   **Publication**: The publication to replicate data from (created in [Step 1](#step-1-create-a-postgres-publication))\\\\n        *   **Destination type**: Select **BigQuery**\\\\n\\\\n    4.  Configure BigQuery-specific settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Project ID**: Your BigQuery project identifier (found in the GCP Console)\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Dataset ID**: The name of your BigQuery dataset (without the project ID)\\\\n\\\\n                <Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n                  In the GCP Console, the dataset is shown as `project-id.dataset-id`. Enter only the part after the dot. For example, if you see `my-project.my_dataset`, enter `my_dataset`.\\\\n                </Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Service Account Key**: Your GCP service account key in JSON format (from Step 1)\\\\n\\\\n    5.  Configure **Advanced Settings** (optional):\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Batch wait time (milliseconds)**: How long to wait for more changes before sending a batch. Default is recommended for optimal performance.\\\\n\\\\n    6.  Click **Create and start** to begin replication\\\\n\\\\n    Your replication pipeline will now start copying data from your database to BigQuery.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How it works\\\\n\\\\n    Once configured, replication to BigQuery:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Captures changes from your Postgres database (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE operations)\\\\n    2.  Batches changes for optimal performance\\\\n    3.  Creates BigQuery tables automatically to match your Postgres schema\\\\n    4.  Streams data to BigQuery\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How tables are structured\\\\n\\\\n    Due to BigQuery limitations, replicated tables use a versioned structure:\\\\n\\\\n    *   The table you query is a **view** (e.g., `users`)\\\\n    *   The actual data is stored in versioned tables with a `_version` suffix (e.g., `users_version`)\\\\n    *   When a table is truncated in your database, a new version is created and the view automatically points to the latest version\\\\n\\\\n    This structure handles table truncations seamlessly while maintaining query compatibility.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Limitations\\\\n\\\\n    *   **Row size**: Limited to 10 MB per row due to BigQuery Storage Write API constraints\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Additional resources\\\\n\\\\n    *   [BigQuery documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs) - Official Google BigQuery documentation\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n</Tabs>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 4: Monitor your pipeline\\\\n\\\\nAfter creating a destination, the replication pipeline will start and appear in the destinations list. You can monitor the pipeline's status and performance from the Dashboard.\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"Replication Destinations List\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-destinations-list.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\nFor comprehensive monitoring instructions including pipeline states, metrics, and logs, see the [Replication Monitoring guide](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-monitoring).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Managing your pipeline\\\\n\\\\nYou can manage your pipeline from the destinations list using the actions menu.\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"Pipeline Actions\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-pipeline-actions.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\nAvailable actions:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Start**: Begin replication for a stopped pipeline\\\\n*   **Stop**: Pause replication (changes will queue up in the WAL)\\\\n*   **Restart**: Stop and start the pipeline (required after publication changes)\\\\n*   **Edit destination**: Modify destination settings like credentials or advanced options\\\\n*   **Delete**: Remove the destination and permanently stop replication\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Adding or removing tables\\\\n\\\\nIf you need to modify which tables are replicated after your replication pipeline is already running, follow these steps:\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  If your Postgres publication uses `FOR ALL TABLES` or `FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA`, new tables in that scope are automatically included in the publication. However, you still **must restart the replication pipeline** for the changes to take effect.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Adding tables to replication\\\\n\\\\n1.  Add the table to your publication using SQL:\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    -- Add a single table to an existing publication\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders add table products;\\\\n\\\\n    -- Or add multiple tables at once\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders add table products, categories;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\\n2.  **Restart the replication pipeline** using the actions menu (see [Managing your pipeline](#managing-your-pipeline)) for the changes to take effect.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Removing tables from replication\\\\n\\\\n1.  Remove the table from your Postgres publication using SQL:\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    -- Remove a single table from a publication\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders drop table orders;\\\\n\\\\n    -- Or remove multiple tables at once\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders drop table orders, products;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\\n2.  **Restart the replication pipeline** using the actions menu (see [Managing your pipeline](#managing-your-pipeline)) for the changes to take effect.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Deleted tables are automatically recreated by the pipeline. To permanently delete a table, pause the pipeline first or remove it from the publication before deleting. See the [FAQ](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq#what-happens-if-a-table-is-deleted-at-the-destination) for details.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### How it works\\\\n\\\\nOnce configured, replication:\\\\n\\\\n1.  **Captures** changes from your Postgres database using Postgres publications and logical replication\\\\n2.  **Streams** the changes through the replication pipeline\\\\n3.  **Loads** the data to your destination in near real-time batches\\\\n\\\\nChanges are sent in batches to optimize performance and reduce costs. The batch size and timing can be adjusted using the advanced settings. The replication pipeline currently performs data extraction and loading only, without transformation - your data is replicated as-is to the destination.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Troubleshooting\\\\n\\\\nIf you encounter issues during setup:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Publication not appearing**: Ensure you created the Postgres publication via SQL and refresh the dashboard\\\\n*   **Tables not showing in publication**: Verify your tables have primary keys (required for Postgres logical replication)\\\\n*   **Pipeline failed to start**: Check the error message in the status view for specific details\\\\n*   **No data being replicated**: Verify your Postgres publication includes the correct tables and event types\\\\n\\\\nFor more troubleshooting help, see the [Replication FAQ](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Limitations\\\\n\\\\nReplication has the following limitations:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Primary keys required**: Tables must have primary keys (Postgres logical replication requirement)\\\\n*   **Custom data types**: Not supported\\\\n*   **Schema changes**: Not automatically handled\\\\n*   **No data transformation**: Data is replicated as-is without transformation\\\\n*   **Data duplicates**: Duplicates can occur when stopping a pipeline if your database has transactions that take longer than a few minutes to complete. See [Can data duplicates occur?](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq#can-data-duplicates-occur-during-pipeline-operations) for details\\\\n\\\\nDestination-specific limitations (such as Iceberg's append-only log format or BigQuery's row size limits) are detailed in each destination tab in [Step 3](#step-3-add-a-destination) above.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Future work\\\\n\\\\nReplication is actively being developed. Planned improvements include:\\\\n\\\\n*   **DDL support**: Automatic handling of Postgres schema changes (ALTER TABLE, ADD COLUMN, etc.)\\\\n*   **Additional destinations**: Support for more data warehouses and analytics platforms\\\\n\\\\nThere are no public timelines for these features, but they represent the roadmap for making replication more robust and flexible.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Next steps\\\\n\\\\n*   [Monitor Replication](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-monitoring)\\\\n*   [View Replication FAQ](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"PGRST106: \\\\\\\"The schema must be one of the following...\\\\\\\" error when querying an exposed schema\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/pgrst106-the-schema-must-be-one-of-the-following-error-when-querying-an-exposed-schema\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# PGRST106: \\\\\\\"The schema must be one of the following...\\\\\\\" error when querying an exposed schema\\\\n\\\\nYou may encounter a `PGRST106` error, stating `{\\\\\\\"code\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"PGRST106\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"message\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"The schema must be one of the following: public\\\\\\\"}`, when attempting to query a schema via the PostgREST API that you've recently exposed.\\\\n\\\\n**Why This Happens:**\\\\nThis error occurs because the `authenticator` role's `pgrst.db_schemas` setting does not include the desired schema. This creates a conflict, as PostgREST relies on this setting to know which schemas it should expose.\\\\n\\\\n**How to Resolve This:**\\\\nTo fix this, you need to update the `pgrst.db_schemas` setting for the `authenticator` role. Connect to your database and execute one of the following SQL commands:\\\\n\\\\n*   **To explicitly add your schema:**\\\\n    If you want to add your specific schema (e.g., `your_schema_name`) alongside existing schemas (like `public`), use the following command. Remember to replace `your_schema_name` with your actual schema name and include all other necessary schemas already defined.\\\\n    `ALTER ROLE authenticator SET pgrst.db_schemas = 'public, your_schema_name';`\\\\n\\\\n*   **To reset to [dashboard configuration](/dashboard/project/_/settings/api):**\\\\n    Alternatively, you can reset this setting to allow the Supabase dashboard's configuration to take effect automatically.\\\\n    `ALTER ROLE authenticator RESET pgrst.db_schemas;`\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Building ChatGPT plugins\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/ai/examples/building-chatgpt-plugins\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Building ChatGPT plugins\\\\n\\\\nUse Supabase as a Retrieval Store for your ChatGPT plugin.\\\\n\\\\nChatGPT recently released [Plugins](https://openai.com/blog/chatgpt-plugins) which help ChatGPT access up-to-date information, run computations, or use third-party services.\\\\nIf you're building a plugin for ChatGPT, you'll probably want to answer questions from a specific source. We can solve this with \\u201cretrieval plugins\\u201d, which allow ChatGPT to access information from a database.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## What is ChatGPT Retrieval Plugin?\\\\n\\\\nA [Retrieval Plugin](https://github.com/openai/chatgpt-retrieval-plugin) is a Python project designed to inject external data into a ChatGPT conversation. It does a few things:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Turn documents into smaller chunks.\\\\n2.  Converts chunks into embeddings using OpenAI's `text-embedding-ada-002` model.\\\\n3.  Stores the embeddings into a vector database.\\\\n4.  Queries the vector database for relevant documents when a question is asked.\\\\n\\\\nIt allows ChatGPT to dynamically pull relevant information into conversations from your data sources. This could be PDF documents, Confluence, or Notion knowledge bases.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Example: Chat with Postgres docs\\\\n\\\\nLet\\u2019s build an example where we can \\u201cask ChatGPT questions\\u201d about the Postgres documentation. Although ChatGPT already knows about the Postgres documentation because it is publicly available, this is a simple example which demonstrates how to work with PDF files.\\\\n\\\\nThis plugin requires several steps:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Download all the [Postgres docs as a PDF](https://www.postgresql.org/files/documentation/pdf/15/postgresql-15-US.pdf)\\\\n2.  Convert the docs into chunks of embedded text and store them in Supabase\\\\n3.  Run our plugin locally so that we can ask questions about the Postgres docs.\\\\n\\\\nWe'll be saving the Postgres documentation in Postgres, and ChatGPT will be retrieving the documentation whenever a user asks a question:\\\\n\\\\n<Image\\\\n  alt=\\\\\\\"diagram reference\\\\\\\"\\\\n  className=\\\\\\\"max-h-[600px]\\\\\\\"\\\\n  src={{\\\\n    light: '/docs/img/ai/chatgpt-plugins/chatgpt-plugin-scheme--light.png',\\\\n    dark: '/docs/img/ai/chatgpt-plugins/chatgpt-plugin-scheme--dark.png',\\\\n  }}\\\\n  zoomable\\\\n/>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 1: Fork the ChatGPT Retrieval Plugin repository\\\\n\\\\nFork the ChatGPT Retrieval Plugin repository to your GitHub account and clone it to your local machine. Read through the `README.md` file to understand the project structure.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 2: Install dependencies\\\\n\\\\nChoose your desired datastore provider and remove unused dependencies from `pyproject.toml`. For this example, we'll use Supabase. And install dependencies with Poetry:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\npoetry install\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 3: Create a Supabase project\\\\n\\\\nCreate a [Supabase project](/dashboard) and database by following the instructions [here](/docs/guides/platform). Export the environment variables required for the retrieval plugin to work:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\nexport OPENAI_API_KEY=<open_ai_api_key>\\\\nexport DATASTORE=supabase\\\\nexport SUPABASE_URL=<supabase_url>\\\\nexport SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=<supabase_key>\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nFor Postgres datastore, you'll need to export these environment variables instead:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\nexport OPENAI_API_KEY=<open_ai_api_key>\\\\nexport DATASTORE=postgres\\\\nexport PG_HOST=<postgres_host_url>\\\\nexport PG_PASSWORD=<postgres_password>\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 4: Run Postgres locally\\\\n\\\\nTo start quicker you may use Supabase CLI to spin everything up locally as it already includes pgvector from the start. Install `supabase-cli`, go to the `examples/providers` folder in the repo and run:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\nsupabase start\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will pull all docker images and run Supabase stack in docker on your local machine. It will also apply all the necessary migrations to set the whole thing up. You can then use your local setup the same way, just export the environment variables and follow to the next steps.\\\\n\\\\nUsing `supabase-cli` is not required and you can use any other docker image or hosted version of Postgres that includes `pgvector`. Just make sure you run migrations from `examples/providers/supabase/migrations/20230414142107_init_pg_vector.sql`.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 5: Obtain OpenAI API key\\\\n\\\\nTo create embeddings Plugin uses OpenAI API and `text-embedding-ada-002` model. Each time we add some data to our datastore, or try to query relevant information from it, embedding will be created either for inserted data chunk, or for the query itself. To make it work we need to export `OPENAI_API_KEY`. If you already have an account in OpenAI, you just need to go to [User Settings - API keys](https://platform.openai.com/account/api-keys) and Create new secret key.\\\\n\\\\n![OpenAI Secret Keys](/docs/img/ai/chatgpt-plugins/openai-secret-keys.png)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 6: Run the plugin\\\\n\\\\nExecute the following command to run the plugin:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\npoetry run dev\\\\n# output\\\\nINFO:     Will watch for changes in these directories: ['./chatgpt-retrieval-plugin']\\\\nINFO:     Uvicorn running on http://localhost:3333 (Press CTRL+C to quit)\\\\nINFO:     Started reloader process [87843] using WatchFiles\\\\nINFO:     Started server process [87849]\\\\nINFO:     Waiting for application startup.\\\\nINFO:     Application startup complete.\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe plugin will start on your localhost - port `:3333` by default.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 6: Populating data in the datastore\\\\n\\\\nFor this example, we'll upload Postgres documentation to the datastore. Download the [Postgres documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/files/documentation/pdf/15/postgresql-15-US.pdf) and use the `/upsert-file` endpoint to upload it:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\ncurl -X POST -F \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"file=@./postgresql-15-US.pdf\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" <http://localhost:3333/upsert-file>\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe plugin will split your data and documents into smaller chunks automatically. You can view the chunks using the Supabase dashboard or any other SQL client you prefer. The entire Postgres Documentation yielded 7,904 records, which is not a lot, but we can try to add index for `embedding` column to speed things up by a little. To do so, you should run the following SQL command:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate index on documents\\\\nusing hnsw (embedding vector_ip_ops)\\\\nwith (lists = 10);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will create an index for the inner product distance function. Important to note that it is an approximate index. It will change the logic from performing the exact nearest neighbor search to the approximate nearest neighbor search.\\\\n\\\\nWe are using `lists = 10`, because as a general guideline, you should start looking for optimal lists constant value with the formula: `rows / 1000` when you have less than 1 million records in your table.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 7: Using our plugin within ChatGPT\\\\n\\\\nTo integrate our plugin with ChatGPT, register it in the ChatGPT dashboard. Assuming you have access to ChatGPT Plugins and plugin development, select the Plugins model in a new chat, then choose \\\\\\\"Plugin store\\\\\\\" and \\\\\\\"Develop your own plugin.\\\\\\\" Enter `localhost:3333` into the domain input, and your plugin is now part of ChatGPT.\\\\n\\\\n![ChatGPT Plugin Store](/docs/img/ai/chatgpt-plugins/chatgpt-plugin-store.png)\\\\n\\\\n![ChatGPT Local Plugin](/docs/img/ai/chatgpt-plugins/chatgpt-local-plugin.png)\\\\n\\\\nYou can now ask questions about Postgres and receive answers derived from the documentation.\\\\n\\\\nLet's try it out: ask ChatGPT to find out when to use `check` and when to use `using`. You will be able to see what queries were sent to our plugin and what it responded to.\\\\n\\\\n![Ask ChatGPT](/docs/img/ai/chatgpt-plugins/ask-chatgpt.png)\\\\n\\\\nAnd after ChatGPT receives a response from the plugin it will answer your question with the data from the documentation.\\\\n\\\\n![ChatGPT Reply](/docs/img/ai/chatgpt-plugins/chatgpt-reply.png)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Resources\\\\n\\\\n*   ChatGPT Retrieval Plugin: [github.com/openai/chatgpt-retrieval-plugin](https://github.com/openai/chatgpt-retrieval-plugin)\\\\n*   ChatGPT Plugins: [official documentation](https://platform.openai.com/docs/plugins/introduction)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Error insufficient privileges         |\\\\n| other                  | 400                            |                                 |\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## API level errors\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Connection errors\\\\n\\\\nErrors that prevent that data API from interacting with Postgres.\\\\n\\\\n| Code     | HTTP status | Description PGRST000 | 503         | Could not connect with the database due to an incorrect connection string or due to the Postgres service not running. |\\\\n| PGRST001 | 503         | Could not connect with arguments:
{"query": "
-- ============================================================
-- POPULATE TABLE 1: gender_statistics
-- ============================================================
INSERT INTO employees.gender_statistics (
    gender,
    total_employees,
    current_employees,
    percentage_of_workforce
)
WITH
  -- Step 1: total headcount per gender (all employees ever hired)
  total_counts AS (
    SELECT
      gender::VARCHAR(1)  AS gender,
      COUNT(*)            AS total_employees
    FROM employees.employee
    GROUP BY gender
  ),
  -- Step 2: current employees = those with an active salary record
  current_active AS (
    SELECT
      e.gender::VARCHAR(1) AS gender,
      COUNT(DISTINCT s.employee_id) AS current_employees
    FROM employees.salary s
    JOIN employees.employee e ON e.id = s.employee_id
    WHERE s.to_date = '9999-01-01'
    GROUP BY e.gender
  ),
  -- Step 3: total current workforce (denominator for percentage)
  current_total AS (
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT employee_id) AS grand_total
    FROM employees.salary
    WHERE to_date = '9999-01-01'
  )
SELECT
  t.gender,
  t.total_employees,
  c.current_employees,
  ROUND(
    (c.current_employees::DECIMAL / ct.grand_total) * 100,
    2
  ) AS percentage_of_workforce
FROM total_counts t
JOIN current_active c  ON c.gender = t.gender
CROSS JOIN current_total ct
ORDER BY t.gender;
"}

{"query": "
-- ============================================================
-- POPULATE TABLE 3: birth_month_distribution
-- ============================================================
INSERT INTO employees.birth_month_distribution (
    birth_month,
    month_name,
    employee_count,
    current_employee_count
)
WITH
  month_names AS (
    SELECT * FROM (VALUES
      (1,'January'),(2,'February'),(3,'March'),(4,'April'),
      (5,'May'),(6,'June'),(7,'July'),(8,'August'),
      (9,'September'),(10,'October'),(11,'November'),(12,'December')
    ) AS mn(birth_month, month_name)
  ),
  -- All employees by birth month
  all_emp AS (
    SELECT
      EXTRACT(MONTH FROM birth_date)::INTEGER AS birth_month,
      COUNT(*) AS employee_count
    FROM employees.employee
    GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM birth_date)::INTEGER
  ),
  -- Current employees (active salary) by birth month
  curr_emp AS (
    SELECT
      EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e.birth_date)::INTEGER AS birth_month,
      COUNT(DISTINCT s.employee_id) AS current_employee_count
    FROM employees.salary s
    JOIN employees.employee e ON e.id = s.employee_id
    WHERE s.to_date = '9999-01-01'
    GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e.birth_date)::INTEGER
  )
SELECT
  mn.birth_month,
  mn.month_name,
  COALESCE(a.employee_count, 0)         AS employee_count,
  COALESCE(c.current_employee_count, 0) AS current_employee_count
FROM month_names mn
LEFT JOIN all_emp  a ON a.birth_month = mn.birth_month
LEFT JOIN curr_emp c ON c.birth_month = mn.birth_month
ORDER BY mn.birth_month;
"}

{"query": "
-- ============================================================
-- POPULATE TABLE 2: age_group_analysis
-- Uses current date to compute age; tenure from hire_date
-- ============================================================
INSERT INTO employees.age_group_analysis (
    age_group,
    employee_count,
    avg_salary,
    avg_tenure_days
)
WITH
  -- Current employees with their active salary
  current_emp AS (
    SELECT
      e.id,
      e.birth_date,
      e.hire_date,
      s.amount AS current_salary,
      -- Age in completed years as of today
      DATE_PART('year', AGE(CURRENT_DATE, e.birth_date))::INTEGER AS age_years,
      -- Tenure in days as of today
      (CURRENT_DATE - e.hire_date)::INTEGER AS tenure_days
    FROM employees.salary s
    JOIN employees.employee e ON e.id = s.employee_id
    WHERE s.to_date = '9999-01-01'
  ),
  -- Assign age group bands
  banded AS (
    SELECT
      CASE
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 20 AND 29 THEN '20-29'
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 30 AND 39 THEN '30-39'
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 40 AND 49 THEN '40-49'
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 50 AND 59 THEN '50-59'
        WHEN age_years >= 60            THEN '60+'
        ELSE 'Other'
      END AS age_group,
      current_salary,
      tenure_days
    FROM current_emp
  )
SELECT
  age_group,
  COUNT(*)                                    AS employee_count,
  ROUND(AVG(current_salary)::DECIMAL, 2)      AS avg_salary,
  ROUND(AVG(tenure_days)::DECIMAL, 2)         AS avg_tenure_days
FROM banded
WHERE age_group <> 'Other'    -- exclude any edge-case outliers
GROUP BY age_group
ORDER BY age_group;
"}

{"query": "
-- ============================================================
-- POPULATE TABLE 4: hiring_year_summary
-- Cohort retention: hired per year vs still active today
-- ============================================================
INSERT INTO employees.hiring_year_summary (
    hire_year,
    employees_hired,
    still_employed,
    retention_rate
)
WITH
  -- All employees with their hire year
  hired AS (
    SELECT
      id,
      EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date)::INTEGER AS hire_year
    FROM employees.employee
  ),
  -- Set of currently active employee IDs
  current_ids AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT employee_id
    FROM employees.salary
    WHERE to_date = '9999-01-01'
  ),
  -- Cohort counts
  cohort AS (
    SELECT
      h.hire_year,
      COUNT(h.id)                                           AS employees_hired,
      COUNT(c.employee_id)                                  AS still_employed
    FROM hired h
    LEFT JOIN current_ids c ON c.employee_id = h.id
    GROUP BY h.hire_year
  )
SELECT
  hire_year,
  employees_hired,
  still_employed,
  ROUND(
    (still_employed::DECIMAL / NULLIF(employees_hired, 0)) * 100,
    2
  ) AS retention_rate
FROM cohort
ORDER BY hire_year;
"}

content.text: The dataset uses 2002 as its logical "present". Birth dates range from 1952–1965, which means ages at reference date (2002) range from ~37–50 years old — perfectly spread across 30-39, 40-49, and 50-59 bands. I'll use `'2002-08-01'` as the reference date and fix the `age_group_analysis` table:

arguments:
{"query": "
-- Clear and re-populate age_group_analysis using dataset reference date 2002-08-01
TRUNCATE employees.age_group_analysis;

INSERT INTO employees.age_group_analysis (
    age_group,
    employee_count,
    avg_salary,
    avg_tenure_days
)
WITH
  -- Reference date: the dataset's logical "today" based on latest salary activity
  ref AS (SELECT DATE '2002-08-01' AS ref_date),
  -- Current employees with their active salary
  current_emp AS (
    SELECT
      e.id,
      e.birth_date,
      e.hire_date,
      s.amount AS current_salary,
      -- Age in completed years as of reference date
      DATE_PART('year', AGE(ref.ref_date, e.birth_date))::INTEGER AS age_years,
      -- Tenure in days from hire_date to reference date
      (ref.ref_date - e.hire_date)::INTEGER AS tenure_days
    FROM employees.salary s
    JOIN employees.employee e ON e.id = s.employee_id
    CROSS JOIN ref
    WHERE s.to_date = '9999-01-01'
  ),
  -- Assign age group bands
  banded AS (
    SELECT
      CASE
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 20 AND 29 THEN '20-29'
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 30 AND 39 THEN '30-39'
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 40 AND 49 THEN '40-49'
        WHEN age_years BETWEEN 50 AND 59 THEN '50-59'
        WHEN age_years >= 60            THEN '60+'
        ELSE 'Other'
      END AS age_group,
      current_salary,
      tenure_days
    FROM current_emp
  )
SELECT
  age_group,
  COUNT(*)                                    AS employee_count,
  ROUND(AVG(current_salary)::DECIMAL, 2)      AS avg_salary,
  ROUND(AVG(tenure_days)::DECIMAL, 2)         AS avg_tenure_days
FROM banded
WHERE age_group <> 'Other'
GROUP BY age_group
ORDER BY age_group;
"}

---

## ✅ Employee Demographics Report — Complete

### What Was Built

Four analytics tables were created in the `employees` schema, each with full column comments and proper primary-key constraints.

---

### 📋 Table 1 — `employees.gender_statistics` (2 rows)

| gender | total_employees | current_employees | percentage_of_workforce |
|--------|----------------|-------------------|------------------------|
| F | 120,051 | 96,010 | **39.98%** |
| M | 179,973 | 144,114 | **60.02%** |

> **Key insight:** The workforce is 60% male and 40% female across both the full historical headcount and the current active workforce — a consistent ratio.

---

### 📋 Table 2 — `employees.age_group_analysis` (3 rows)

Age computed relative to the dataset's reference date (2002-08-01):

| age_group | employee_count | avg_salary | avg_tenure_days |
|-----------|---------------|------------|-----------------|
| 30-39 | 46,050 | $72,016.48 | 4,569.72 days (~12.5 yrs) |
| 40-49 | 184,705 | $72,017.06 | 4,565.58 days (~12.5 yrs) |
| 50-59 | 9,369 | $71,896.27 | 4,558.34 days (~12.5 yrs) |

> **Key insight:** The 40-49 band dominates the workforce (77%). Average salary is remarkably consistent (~$72K) across all age groups. Tenure averages ~12.5 years for all bands.

---

### 📋 Table 3 — `employees.birth_month_distribution` (12 rows)

All 12 months are covered. Birth months are very evenly distributed:

| Highlights | Value |
|---|---|
| Highest month | July — 20,535 current employees |
| Lowest month | February — 18,759 current employees |
| Range spread | Only ~1,776 employees between high/low — very uniform |

> **Key insight:** No statistically significant birth-month clustering — distribution is essentially uniform across the year.

---

### 📋 Table 4 — `employees.hiring_year_summary` (16 rows, 1985–2000)

| Highlights | Value |
|---|---|
| Peak hiring year | 1986 — 36,150 hired |
| Consistent retention | ~79–80% across nearly all cohorts |
| Best retention | 1993 cohort — 80.90% |
| Most recent (2000) | Only 13 hires, 69.23% retained |

> **Key insight:** The company maintained an extremely stable ~80% retention rate across 15 years of hiring cohorts (1985–1999). The 2000 cohort is statistically small (13 employees) so its 69% rate is not significant.

---

### 🔑 Design Decisions

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Active salary filter** | `to_date = '9999-01-01'` is the canonical "currently employed" marker in this schema |
| **Reference date for age** | Used `2002-08-01` (max salary activity date) instead of `CURRENT_DATE` — the dataset is historical, born 1952–1965, so using today would place everyone in "60+" |
| **Primary keys on all tables** | Enables PostgREST auto-API access and prevents duplicate inserts |
| **Column comments** | Every column has a `COMMENT ON COLUMN` for self-documentation in the Supabase dashboard |
| **DECIMAL precision** | Percentages at 2dp, salaries at 2dp, tenure days at 2dp — all appropriate for HR reporting |
